title: Constants and Immutable Values
learningObjectives: Explain the key idea in constants and immutable values.
Identify suitable syntax and type/value rules.
Trace each example and predict the result.
Use the concept in a small practical program.
Avoid a common mistake related to initialization, constness or type choice.

understand.concept: A constant is a value or object that code is not allowed to modify through that name after initialization. C++ uses const for compile-time or runtime initialized constants and constexpr for values that can be evaluated at compile time when requirements are met. Constants clarify intent and prevent accidental changes.
understand.whyItMatters: These fundamentals appear in nearly every C++ program and help make code predictable, readable and correct.
understand.analogy: Think of a labeled container: its label identifies what it is meant to hold, and its rules determine what can be put inside or changed.
understand.analogyLimit: Real C++ types have language-defined rules, conversions, representation and lifetime that a physical container analogy cannot capture.
understand.explain:
## const
`const` makes an object non-modifiable through that name after initialization. It must be initialized when declared.

## constexpr
`constexpr` expresses that a value or function is usable in constant-expression contexts when the language rules and inputs allow it. Use it for values that truly belong at compile time.

## Choose meaningful names
Constants often use descriptive names. Naming style varies by project; follow local conventions consistently.

examples.title: A const value
examples.explanation: The const object cannot be reassigned.

examples.title: A compile-time constant
examples.explanation: constexpr marks a value intended to be constant-evaluated.

examples.title: Use a constant in a calculation
examples.code: const double taxRate{0.05};\ndouble tax{100.0 * taxRate};\nstd::cout << tax;
examples.explanation: A named constant makes the formula easier to understand.

examples.title: Attempted modification (invalid)
examples.code: const int limit{10};\n// limit = 12; // not allowed
examples.explanation: This deliberately shows an invalid modification.

examples.title: Function with constexpr
examples.code: constexpr int triple(int n){ return n*3; }\nconstexpr int result{triple(4)};
examples.explanation: A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time for suitable inputs.
